title: CHAPTER NINE. On the infinity of God; extensive and intensive
latin: CAPUT NONUM, De infinitate Dei. Atque haec de primo Dei attributo, nempe absoluta exsistendi necessitate: sequitur alterum, nimirum I. Infinitas, quae hic est, summa essentiae divinae perfectio, omni termino ac limite carens. INFINITATIS vocabulum hic mutuamur ab iis, quae quantitati alias proprie tribuuntur. Dicitur autem Deus duobus modis perfectionis suae termino carere, extensive videlicet & intensive. Extensive, quia ejus natura non est praecise limitata ad unum genus perfectionum, sed in se concludit omnia perfectionum genera, quaecunque cogitari aut esse ullo modo possunt, idque in infinitum. Atque ita Deus simpliciter & absolute perfectus dicitur, quia omnis perfectio illi ita necessario inest, ut nulla prorsus illi deesse queat.
english: CHAPTER NINE. On the infinity of God.

And these things concerning the first attribute of God, namely absolute necessity of existing: there follows the second, namely I. Infinity, which here is the highest perfection of the divine essence, lacking every term and limit. The vocabulary of INFINITY we here borrow from those things which otherwise are properly attributed to quantity.

But God is said in two ways to lack a term of His perfection, namely extensively and intensively. Extensively, because His nature is not precisely limited to one genus of perfections, but in itself encloses all genera of perfections whatever can be thought or be in any way, and that infinitely. And so God is called simply and absolutely perfect, because every perfection so necessarily inheres in Him that none at all can be lacking to Him.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): CHAPTER NINE. Concerning ye infinity belonging toward God. And these things concerning ye first attribute belonging toward God, namely absolute necessity belonging toward existing: ye second follows, namely I. Infinity, which here ye highest perfection belonging toward ye divine essence, every term plus limit lacking, is. Ye vocabulary belonging toward INFINITY here from those things which otherwise properly unto quantity are attributed we borrow. But God in two ways a term belonging toward His perfection to lack is said, namely extensively plus intensively. Extensively, because His nature precisely unto one genus belonging toward perfections limited is not, but in itself all genera belonging toward perfections whatever thought or in any way be can encloses, plus that infinitely. And so God simply plus absolutely perfect is called, because every perfection so necessarily in Him inheres that none at all unto Him can be lacking.

title: Formal ratio of infinity; proper to God alone
latin: Formale consistit in negatione termini, qui est, tum quaelibet entis perfectio, cum praecisione caeterarum perfectionum, tum quilibet perfectionis gradus, cum praecisione reliquorum graduum. Haec vero proprietas ita Deo convenit, ut in nulla creaturarum inveniatur, quia omnis creatura necessario certum definitumque perfectionum numerum, earumque omnium definitum ac limitatum gradum a Deo omnis perfectionis fonte capit.
english: The formal consists in the negation of a term, which is both any perfection of a being with the precision of the other perfections, and any grade of perfection with the precision of the remaining grades. But this property so belongs to God that it is found in none of the creatures, because every creature necessarily takes from God the fountain of every perfection a certain and definite number of perfections, and of all of them a definite and limited grade.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): Ye formal in ye negation belonging toward a term consists, which both any perfection belonging toward a being with ye precision belonging toward ye other perfections is, plus any grade belonging toward perfection with ye precision belonging toward ye remaining grades. But this property so unto God belongs that in none belonging toward ye creatures it is found, because every creature necessarily from God ye fountain belonging toward every perfection a certain plus definite number belonging toward perfections, plus of all of them a definite plus limited grade, takes.

title: Proofs 1–2: Scripture; infinite goodness
latin: PRIMO, sacrae Scripturae testimoniis, quae Deo magnitudinem & excellentiam supra omnes res creatas attribuunt, Job. 36.26 & 37.23; Psal. 48.2 & 95.3 & 96.4 & 97.9 & 99.2 & 145.3; Tit. 2.13 & alibi passim. SECUNDO, a summa Dei bonitate. Talis bonitas necessario est aeternis indefecta, adeoque infinita: cum omnis finita bonitas necessario deficiat a summa bonitate. Unde Gregorius Nyssenus libro de opificio hominis cap. 1. docet, Deum esse bonum, omne bonum, quod intelligendo cogitandoque comprehenditur, exsuperans, hoc est, infinitum.
english: FIRST, by the testimonies of sacred Scripture, which attribute to God greatness and excellence above all created things (Job 36:26 and 37:23; Psalm 48:2 and 95:3 and 96:4 and 97:9 and 99:2 and 145:3; Titus 2:13 and elsewhere everywhere).

SECOND, from God's highest goodness. Such goodness is necessarily undefective for eternities, and therefore infinite: since every finite goodness necessarily falls short of the highest goodness. From which Gregory of Nyssa (On the Making of Man, chapter 1) teaches that God is good, surpassing every good which is comprehended by understanding and thinking — that is, infinite.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): FIRST, by ye testimonies belonging toward sacred Scripture, which unto God greatness plus excellence above all created things attribute (Job 36:26 plus 37:23; Psalm 48:2 plus 95:3 plus 96:4 plus 97:9 plus 99:2 plus 145:3; Titus 2:13 plus elsewhere everywhere). SECOND, from God's highest goodness. Such goodness necessarily for eternities undefective is, plus therefore infinite: since every finite goodness necessarily from ye highest goodness falls short. From which Gregory belonging toward Nyssa (On ye Making belonging toward Man, chapter 1) teaches that God good is, every good which by understanding plus thinking is comprehended surpassing — that is, infinite.

title: Proofs 3–4: nothing greater than God; first being contains all perfection
latin: TERTIO, Deum extensive & intensive infinitum esse ita evinco. Omni ente finito potest aliud esse perfectius & majus. Deo nihil potest esse perfectius & majus. Ergo Deus non est ens finitum. QUARTO, Deus habet omnem entis perfectionem, quia absolutum primum, unde caetera omnia dependent, necessario perfectione sua excedit reliqua omnia entia. Ergo omnem eorum perfectionem eminentiori modo in se continet, et potentia quae numquam ita exhauriri possunt ut non novas rerum species & perfectiones depromere possint.
english: THIRD, I prove that God is extensively and intensively infinite thus. For every finite being something else can be more perfect and greater. For God nothing can be more perfect and greater. Therefore God is not a finite being.

FOURTH, God has every perfection of being, because the absolute first, on which all the rest depend, necessarily exceeds all remaining beings by His perfection. Therefore He contains every perfection of theirs in Himself in a more eminent manner, and powers which can never be so exhausted that they cannot bring forth new species and perfections of things.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): THIRD, that God extensively plus intensively infinite is thus I prove. For every finite being something else more perfect plus greater can be. For God nothing more perfect plus greater can be. Therefore God a finite being is not. FOURTH, God every perfection belonging toward being has, because ye absolute first, on which all ye rest depend, necessarily by His perfection all remaining beings exceeds. Therefore every perfection belonging toward theirs in Himself in a more eminent manner He contains, plus powers which never so exhausted can be that new species plus perfections belonging toward things they cannot bring forth.

title: Proof 5: intensive infinity from aseity; joined with affirmative attributes
latin: QUINTO, omnem essentiae perfectionem, quae in Deo est, esse quoque intensive infinitam, hoc est, sine mensura & termino illi inesse, ita ostendo. Ens a seipso exsistens ex necessitate naturae suae, nequit esse limitatum ad certum perfectionis gradum. Atqui Deus est ens a seipso exsistens ex necessitate naturae suae, ut cap. 8. demonstratum fuit. Ergo Deus nequit esse limitatus ad certum perfectionis gradum. Atque ex hoc non tantum infinitatem Deo tribuimus absolute, sed etiam eam cum aliis attributis, praesertim affirmativis, conjungimus, ut, quando sapientiam, potentiam, bonitatem infinitam in Deo esse dicimus.
english: FIFTH, that every perfection of essence which is in God is also intensively infinite — that is, inheres in Him without measure and term — I show thus. A being existing from itself by the necessity of its nature cannot be limited to a certain grade of perfection. But God is a being existing from itself by the necessity of its nature, as was demonstrated in chapter 8. Therefore God cannot be limited to a certain grade of perfection.
And from this we attribute infinity to God not only absolutely, but also join it with other attributes, especially affirmative ones, as when we say infinite wisdom, power, and goodness are in God.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): FIFTH, that every perfection belonging toward essence which in God is also intensively infinite is — that is, without measure plus term in Him inheres — thus I show. A being from itself by ye necessity belonging toward its nature existing unto a certain grade belonging toward perfection limited cannot be. But God a being from itself by ye necessity belonging toward its nature existing is, as in chapter 8 was demonstrated. Therefore God unto a certain grade belonging toward perfection limited cannot be. And from this infinity unto God not only absolutely we attribute, but also with other attributes, especially affirmative ones, we join it, as when infinite wisdom, power, plus goodness in God are we say.

title: Proof 7: orthodox antiquity and pagan witnesses — Cap. 9 close
latin: SEPTIMO, consensu & autoritate orthodoxae antiquitatis. Dionysius libro de divinis nominibus cap. 5: Unitas, ait, continet Deus, secundum supersubstantialem simplicem infinitatem suam. Damascenus lib. 1. orthod. fidei cap. 12: Universum, ait, id quod est, tanquam immensum quoddam & infinitum essentiae pelagus complexu suo continet. Bernhardus: Hoc Deo est esse, quod haec omnia esse. Mercurius Trismegistus Deum vocat Bonum interminatum & infinitum. Orpheus Deum appellat infinitum finem. Sic Xenophanes, Parmenides, Melissus dicunt, id quod est, nempe Deum, infinitum esse.
english: SEVENTH, by the consensus and authority of orthodox antiquity. Dionysius (On the Divine Names, chapter 5): Unity, he says, God contains according to His supersubstantial simple infinity. Damascene (Orthodox Faith 1.12): The universe, he says, that which is, as a certain immense and infinite sea of essence He contains in His embrace. Bernard: For God this is to be, which is to be all these things. Mercury Trismegistus calls God the interminable and infinite Good. Orpheus calls God the infinite end. So Xenophanes, Parmenides, Melissus say that that which is — namely God — is infinite.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): SEVENTH, by ye consensus plus authority belonging toward orthodox antiquity. Dionysius (On ye Divine Names, chapter 5): Unity, he says, God according to His supersubstantial simple infinity contains. Damascene (Orthodox Faith 1.12): Ye universe, he says, that which is, as a certain immense plus infinite sea belonging toward essence in His embrace He contains. Bernard: For God this to be is, which all these things to be is. Mercury Trismegistus God ye interminable plus infinite Good calls. Orpheus God ye infinite end calls. So Xenophanes, Parmenides, Melissus say that that which is — namely God — infinite is.
